catalog_quote: 2.4. Word stress and stress shift. Yakan words have three degrees of stress: primary, secondary, and weak stress. A polysyllabic word has one primary stress; if a word has more than three syllables, it also has a secondary stress. Syllables with neither primary nor secondary stress, including monosyllabic words, carry weak stress. Primary stress is predictable and always occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. Secondary stress is also predictable and always occurs on the second syllable to the left of the one bearing primary stress. Suffixation causes stress to shift one syllable to the right, as shown in (4). (In order to avoid confusion with the orthographic symbol for a glottal stop, primary stress is indicated by the symbol " which precedes the stressed syllable.) (4) "luma' 'house' lu"ma'in 'house' (definite); La"mitan 'name of a place' Lami"tanin 'Lamitan' (definite); ala"…

sources.quote: 'Word stress in Yakan is predictable. There are three degrees of stress: primary, secondary and weak stress. A polysyllabic word has one primary stress; if a word has more than three syllables, it also has a secondary stress. ... Primary stress always occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. In words with four or five syllables, secondary stress always comes two syllables before the primary stress. Suffixation (always one syllable) causes stress to shift one syllable to the right.'
sources.locator: printed p. 3, 'Word stress and shift' (PDF page 2)
sources.note: Third statement of the rule by the same fieldworker, adds 'Suffixation (always one syllable)'; useful as a corroborating citation. fetched sources now; confirms.
